    18	
    19	PyPSA stands for "Python for Power System Analysis". It is pronounced
    20	"pipes-ah".
    21	
    22	PyPSA is an open source toolbox for simulating and optimising modern power and
    23	energy systems that include features such as conventional generators with unit
    24	commitment, variable wind and solar generation, storage units, coupling to other
    25	energy sectors, and mixed alternating and direct current networks. PyPSA is
    26	designed to scale well with large networks and long time series.
    27	
    28	This project is maintained by the [Department of Digital Transformation in
    29	Energy Systems](https://tub-ensys.github.io) at the [Technical University of
    30	Berlin](https://www.tu.berlin). Previous versions were developed by the Energy
    31	System Modelling group at the [Institute for Automation and Applied
    32	Informatics](https://www.iai.kit.edu/english/index.php) at the [Karlsruhe
    33	Institute of Technology](http://www.kit.edu/english/index.php) funded by the
    34	[Helmholtz Association](https://www.helmholtz.de/en/), and by the [Renewable
    35	Energy
    36	Group](https://fias.uni-frankfurt.de/physics/schramm/renewable-energy-system-and-network-analysis/)
    37	at [FIAS](https://fias.uni-frankfurt.de/) to carry out simulations for the
    38	[CoNDyNet project](http://condynet.de/), financed by the [German Federal
    39	Ministry for Education and Research (BMBF)](https://www.bmbf.de/en/index.html)
    40	as part of the [Stromnetze Research
    41	Initiative](http://forschung-stromnetze.info/projekte/grundlagen-und-konzepte-fuer-effiziente-dezentrale-stromnetze/).
    42	
    43	## Functionality
    44	
    45	PyPSA can calculate:
    46	
    47	-   static power flow (using both the full non-linear network equations and the
    48	    linearised network equations)
    49	-   linear optimal power flow (least-cost optimisation of power plant and
    50	    storage dispatch within network constraints, using the linear network
    51	    equations, over several snapshots)
    52	-   security-constrained linear optimal power flow
    53	-   total electricity/energy system least-cost investment optimisation (using
    54	    linear network equations, over several snapshots and investment periods
    55	    simultaneously for optimisation of generation and storage dispatch and
    56	    investment in the capacities of generation, storage, transmission and other
    57	    infrastructure)
    58	
    59	It has models for:
    60	
    61	-   meshed multiply-connected AC and DC networks, with controllable converters
    62	    between AC and DC networks
    63	-   standard types for lines and transformers following the implementation in
    64	    [pandapower](https://www.pandapower.org/)
    65	-   conventional dispatchable generators and links with unit commitment
    66	-   generators with time-varying power availability, such as wind and solar
    67	    generators
    68	-   storage units with efficiency losses
    69	-   simple hydroelectricity with inflow and spillage
    70	-   coupling with other energy carriers (e.g. resistive Power-to-Heat (P2H),
    71	    Power-to-Gas (P2G), battery electric vehicles (BEVs), Fischer-Tropsch,
    72	    direct air capture (DAC))
    73	-   basic components out of which more complicated assets can be built, such as
    74	    Combined Heat and Power (CHP) units and heat pumps.
    75	
    76	## Documentation
    77	
    78	[Documentation](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html)
    79	
    80	[Quick start](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quick_start.html)
    81	
    82	[Examples](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples-basic.html)
    83	
    84	[Known users of
    85	PyPSA](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users.html)
    86	
    87	## Installation
    88	
    89	pip:
    90	
    91	```pip install pypsa```
    92	
    93	conda/mamba:
    94	
    95	```conda install -c conda-forge pypsa```
    96	
    97	Additionally, install a solver.
    98	
    99	## Usage
   100	
   101	```py
   102	import pypsa
   103	
   104	# create a new network
   105	n = pypsa.Network()
   106	n.add("Bus", "mybus")
   107	n.add("Load", "myload", bus="mybus", p_set=100)
   108	n.add("Generator", "mygen", bus="mybus", p_nom=100, marginal_cost=20)
   109	
   110	# load an example network
   111	n = pypsa.examples.ac_dc_meshed()
   112	
   113	# run the optimisation
   114	n.optimize()
   115	
   116	# plot results
   117	n.generators_t.p.plot()
   118	n.plot()
   119	
   120	# get statistics
   121	n.statistics()
   122	n.statistics.energy_balance()
   123	```
   124	
   125	There are [more extensive
   126	examples](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples-basic.html) available
   127	as [Jupyter notebooks](https://jupyter.org/). They are also described in the
   128	[doc/examples.rst](doc/examples.rst) and are available as Python scripts in
   129	[examples/](examples/).

   131	## Screenshots

   145	
   146	## Dependencies
   147	
   148	PyPSA is written and tested to be compatible with Python 3.7 and above.
   149	The last release supporting Python 2.7 was PyPSA 0.15.0.
   150	
   151	It leans heavily on the following Python packages:
   152	
   153	-   [pandas](http://pandas.pydata.org/) for storing data about
   154	    components and time series
   155	-   [numpy](http://www.numpy.org/) and [scipy](http://scipy.org/) for
   156	    calculations, such as linear algebra and sparse matrix calculations
   157	-   [networkx](https://networkx.github.io/) for some network
   158	    calculations
   159	-   [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/) for static plotting
   160	-   [linpy](https://github.com/PyPSA/linopy) for preparing optimisation problems
   161	    (currently only linear and mixed integer linear optimisation)
   162	-   [cartopy](https://scitools.org.uk/cartopy) for plotting the
   163	    baselayer map
   164	-   [pytest](http://pytest.org/) for unit testing
   165	-   [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) for
   166	    managing messages

   168	The optimisation uses interface libraries like `linopy` which are
   169	independent of the preferred solver. You can use e.g. one of the free
   170	solvers [GLPK](https://www.gnu.org/software/glpk/) and
   171	[CLP/CBC](https://github.com/coin-or/Cbc/) or the commercial solver
   172	[Gurobi](http://www.gurobi.com/) for which free academic licenses are

This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value
3. Simple activities completable in minimal steps
4. Pure information exchange or discussion

Note: For single straightforward tasks, proceed with direct implementation
rather than creating tracking overhead.

## Usage Scenarios

**Scenario A: Feature Development with Validation**
User request: "Build a user authentication system with login/logout functionality.
Don't forget to include input validation and error handling!"

Response approach: I'll implement a user authentication system with comprehensive
validation. Let me organize this work systematically.

*Task breakdown includes:*
1. Design authentication API endpoints and data models
2. Implement user login/logout controllers with session management
3. Add client-side form validation and error display
4. Create backend input sanitization and security checks
5. Implement comprehensive error handling for edge cases
6. Perform integration testing and fix any issues

**Scenario B: Codebase Refactoring**
User request: "I need to update all instances of the method 'fetchData' to
'retrieveInformation' throughout the entire project"

Response approach: Let me first analyze your codebase to identify all locations
where 'fetchData' appears.

*After code analysis*

I've located 12 occurrences of 'fetchData' across 6 files in your project.
I'll create a systematic plan to update these references.

*Organized task list includes specific file-by-file updates*

**Scenario C: Multi-feature Development**
User request: "Set up a blog platform with these components: admin dashboard,
article management, comment system, and user profiles."

Response approach: I'll help build your blog platform. Let me break down these
components into manageable implementation phases.

*Creates structured plan with each feature decomposed into specific development tasks*

## Counter-examples - Direct Implementation Preferred

**Counter-example A: Simple inquiry**
User request: "What's the syntax for a for loop in JavaScript?"

Response approach: Here's how to write a for loop in JavaScript:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    console.log(array[i]);
}
```

*No task tracking needed - single informational response*

**Counter-example B: Minor modification**
User request: "Please add a docstring to the processPayment function explaining
its parameters."

Response approach: I'll add a docstring to explain the processPayment function.

*Direct edit without task tracking for simple modification*

## Status Management and Workflow

1. **Status Values**: Track work using these states:
   - todo: Not yet initiated
   - in_progress: Currently active (maintain single focus)
   - done: Successfully completed

2. **Workflow Practices**:
   - Update status dynamically as work progresses
   - Mark completion immediately upon task finish
   - Limit active work to ONE task at any given time
   - Complete current activities before initiating new ones
   - Remove obsolete tasks from tracking entirely

3. **Completion Criteria**:
   - Mark tasks as done only when fully achieved
   - Keep status as in_progress if errors, blocks, or partial completion exist
   - Create new tasks for discovered issues or dependencies
   - Never mark done when:
       - Test suites are failing
       - Implementation remains incomplete
       - Unresolved errors persist
       - Required resources are unavailable

4. **Task Organization**:
   - Write precise, actionable descriptions
   - Decompose complex work into manageable units
   - Use descriptive, clear naming conventions

When uncertain, favor using this tool. Proactive task management demonstrates
systematic approach and ensures comprehensive requirement fulfillment.

Perfect! I've successfully reproduced the issue. The error is exactly as described: `TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not Dataset`.

## Phase 5. FIX ANALYSIS

arguments.thought:
Let me clearly analyze the problem and solution:

5.1 What the problem is:
The `import_from_netcdf` function in `/workspace/PyPSA__PyPSA__0.25/pypsa/io.py` at line 656 unconditionally tries to create a `Path(path)` object. When `path` is an xarray Dataset instance, this fails with a TypeError because Path() constructor expects a string or path-like object.

5.2 Where the problem is located:
File: `/workspace/PyPSA__PyPSA__0.25/pypsa/io.py`
Function: `import_from_netcdf` (lines 642-659)
Specific problematic line: Line 656: `basename = Path(path).name`

5.3 How the test reproduces the issue:
The test creates a Network, exports it to netcdf (which returns an xarray Dataset), then tries to import that Dataset into another Network. This triggers the TypeError when `import_from_netcdf` tries to create `Path(path)` where path is a Dataset.

5.4 Best practices to consider:
- Maintain backward compatibility with existing file path usage
- Handle both string/Path inputs and xarray Dataset inputs properly
- The ImporterNetCDF class already correctly handles both cases, so we just need to fix the basename extraction
- Don't duplicate logic that already exists in ImporterNetCDF

5.5 How to fix the problem:
The fix is to conditionally extract the basename only when the path is a string or Path-like object. When it's an xarray Dataset, we can either:
- Use a default basename like "dataset" 
- Extract some meaningful name from the Dataset if possible
- Pass None as basename

Looking at the `_import_from_importer` function call, the basename is used for logging purposes. Since xarray Datasets don't have filenames, using a generic name like "dataset" or the Dataset's name attribute (if it exists) would be appropriate.

Looking at the ImporterNetCDF.__init__ method, it correctly handles both cases:
- For string/Path: opens the dataset and stores both path and ds
- For Dataset: stores the dataset directly as ds

The issue is just that we're forcing Path conversion on line 656 regardless of the input type.

    13	[![pre-commit.ci status](https://results.pre-commit.ci/badge/github/PyPSA/PyPSA/master.svg)](https://results.pre-commit.ci/latest/github/PyPSA/PyPSA/master)
    14	[![Code style: black](https://img.shields.io/badge/code%20style-black-000000.svg)](https://github.com/psf/black)
    15	[![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/911692131440148490?logo=discord)](https://discord.gg/AnuJBk23FU)
    16	[![Contributor Covenant](https://img.shields.io/badge/Contributor%20Covenant-2.1-4baaaa.svg)](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
    17	[![Stack Exchange questions](https://img.shields.io/stackexchange/stackoverflow/t/pypsa)](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/pypsa)
    18	
    19	PyPSA stands for "Python for Power System Analysis". It is pronounced
    20	"pipes-ah".
    21	
    22	PyPSA is an open source toolbox for simulating and optimising modern power and
    23	energy systems that include features such as conventional generators with unit
    24	commitment, variable wind and solar generation, storage units, coupling to other
    25	energy sectors, and mixed alternating and direct current networks. PyPSA is
    26	designed to scale well with large networks and long time series.
    27	
    28	This project is maintained by the [Department of Digital Transformation in
    29	Energy Systems](https://tub-ensys.github.io) at the [Technical University of
    30	Berlin](https://www.tu.berlin). Previous versions were developed by the Energy
    31	System Modelling group at the [Institute for Automation and Applied
    32	Informatics](https://www.iai.kit.edu/english/index.php) at the [Karlsruhe
    33	Institute of Technology](http://www.kit.edu/english/index.php) funded by the
    34	[Helmholtz Association](https://www.helmholtz.de/en/), and by the [Renewable
    35	Energy
    36	Group](https://fias.uni-frankfurt.de/physics/schramm/renewable-energy-system-and-network-analysis/)
    37	at [FIAS](https://fias.uni-frankfurt.de/) to carry out simulations for the
    38	[CoNDyNet project](http://condynet.de/), financed by the [German Federal
    39	Ministry for Education and Research (BMBF)](https://www.bmbf.de/en/index.html)
    40	as part of the [Stromnetze Research
    41	Initiative](http://forschung-stromnetze.info/projekte/grundlagen-und-konzepte-fuer-effiziente-dezentrale-stromnetze/).
    42	
    43	## Functionality
    44	
    45	PyPSA can calculate:
    46	
    47	-   static power flow (using both the full non-linear network equations and the
    48	    linearised network equations)
    49	-   linear optimal power flow (least-cost optimisation of power plant and
    50	    storage dispatch within network constraints, using the linear network
    51	    equations, over several snapshots)
    52	-   security-constrained linear optimal power flow
    53	-   total electricity/energy system least-cost investment optimisation (using
    54	    linear network equations, over several snapshots and investment periods
    55	    simultaneously for optimisation of generation and storage dispatch and
    56	    investment in the capacities of generation, storage, transmission and other
    57	    infrastructure)
    58	
    59	It has models for:
    60	
    61	-   meshed multiply-connected AC and DC networks, with controllable converters
    62	    between AC and DC networks
    63	-   standard types for lines and transformers following the implementation in
    64	    [pandapower](https://www.pandapower.org/)
    65	-   conventional dispatchable generators and links with unit commitment
    66	-   generators with time-varying power availability, such as wind and solar
    67	    generators
    68	-   storage units with efficiency losses
    69	-   simple hydroelectricity with inflow and spillage
    70	-   coupling with other energy carriers (e.g. resistive Power-to-Heat (P2H),
    71	    Power-to-Gas (P2G), battery electric vehicles (BEVs), Fischer-Tropsch,
    72	    direct air capture (DAC))
    73	-   basic components out of which more complicated assets can be built, such as
    74	    Combined Heat and Power (CHP) units and heat pumps.
    75	
    76	## Documentation
    77	
    78	[Documentation](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html)
    79	
    80	[Quick start](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quick_start.html)
    81	
    82	[Examples](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples-basic.html)
    83	
    84	[Known users of
    85	PyPSA](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/users.html)
    86	
    87	## Installation
    88	
    89	pip:
    90	
    91	```pip install pypsa```
    92	
    93	conda/mamba:
    94	
    95	```conda install -c conda-forge pypsa```
    96	
    97	Additionally, install a solver.
    98	
    99	## Usage
   100	
   101	```py
   102	import pypsa
   103	
   104	# create a new network
   105	n = pypsa.Network()
   106	n.add("Bus", "mybus")
   107	n.add("Load", "myload", bus="mybus", p_set=100)
   108	n.add("Generator", "mygen", bus="mybus", p_nom=100, marginal_cost=20)
   109	
   110	# load an example network
   111	n = pypsa.examples.ac_dc_meshed()
   112	
   113	# run the optimisation
   114	n.optimize()
   115	
   116	# plot results
   117	n.generators_t.p.plot()
   118	n.plot()
   119	
   120	# get statistics
   121	n.statistics()
   122	n.statistics.energy_balance()
   123	```
   124	
   125	There are [more extensive
   126	examples](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/examples-basic.html) available
   127	as [Jupyter notebooks](https://jupyter.org/). They are also described in the
   128	[doc/examples.rst](doc/examples.rst) and are available as Python scripts in
   129	[examples/](examples/).
   130	
   131	## Screenshots
   132	
   133	[PyPSA-Eur](https://github.com/PyPSA/pypsa-eur) optimising capacities of
   134	generation, storage and transmission lines (9% line volume expansion allowed)
   135	for a 95% reduction in CO2 emissions in Europe compared to 1990 levels
   136	
   137	![image](doc/img/elec_s_256_lv1.09_Co2L-3H.png)
   138	
   139	[SciGRID model](https://power.scigrid.de/) simulating the German power system
   140	for 2015.
   141	
   142	![image](doc/img/stacked-gen_and_storage-scigrid.png)
   143	
   144	![image](doc/img/lmp_and_line-loading.png)
   145	
   146	## Dependencies
   147	
   148	PyPSA is written and tested to be compatible with Python 3.7 and above.
   149	The last release supporting Python 2.7 was PyPSA 0.15.0.
   150	
   151	It leans heavily on the following Python packages:
   152	
   153	-   [pandas](http://pandas.pydata.org/) for storing data about
   154	    components and time series
   155	-   [numpy](http://www.numpy.org/) and [scipy](http://scipy.org/) for
   156	    calculations, such as linear algebra and sparse matrix calculations
   157	-   [networkx](https://networkx.github.io/) for some network
   158	    calculations
   159	-   [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/) for static plotting
   160	-   [linpy](https://github.com/PyPSA/linopy) for preparing optimisation problems
   161	    (currently only linear and mixed integer linear optimisation)
   162	-   [cartopy](https://scitools.org.uk/cartopy) for plotting the
   163	    baselayer map
   164	-   [pytest](http://pytest.org/) for unit testing
   165	-   [logging](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) for
   166	    managing messages
   167	
   168	The optimisation uses interface libraries like `linopy` which are
   169	independent of the preferred solver. You can use e.g. one of the free
   170	solvers [GLPK](https://www.gnu.org/software/glpk/) and
   171	[CLP/CBC](https://github.com/coin-or/Cbc/) or the commercial solver
   172	[Gurobi](http://www.gurobi.com/) for which free academic licenses are
   173	available.
   174	
   175	## Documentation
   176	
   177	Please check the [documentation](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io).
   178	
   179	## Contributing and Support
   180	
   181	We strongly welcome anyone interested in contributing to this project. If you have any ideas, suggestions or encounter problems, feel invited to file issues or make pull requests on GitHub.
   182	
   183	-   In case of code-related **questions**, please post on [stack overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/pypsa).
   184	-   For non-programming related and more general questions please refer to the [mailing list](https://groups.google.com/group/pypsa).
   185	-   To **discuss** with other PyPSA users, organise projects, share news, and get in touch with the community you can use the [discord server](https://discord.gg/AnuJBk23FU).
   186	-   For **bugs and feature requests**, please use the [PyPSA Github Issues page](https://github.com/PyPSA/PyPSA/issues).
   187	-   For **troubleshooting**, please check the [troubleshooting](https://pypsa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/troubleshooting.html) in the documentation.
   188	
   189	## Code of Conduct
   190	
   191	Please respect our [code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
   192	
   193	## Citing PyPSA
   194	
   195	If you use PyPSA for your research, we would appreciate it if you would
   196	cite the following paper:
   197	
   198	-   T. Brown, J. Hörsch, D. Schlachtberger, [PyPSA: Python for Power
   199	    System Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.09913), 2018, [Journal
   200	    of Open Research
   201	    Software](https://openresearchsoftware.metajnl.com/), 6(1),
   202	    [arXiv:1707.09913](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.09913),

5.1 What the problem is:
The `import_from_netcdf` function in `/workspace/PyPSA__PyPSA__0.25/pypsa/io.py` at line 656 unconditionally tries to create a `Path(path)` object. When `path` is an xarray Dataset instance, this fails with a TypeError because Path() constructor expects a string or path-like object.

5.2 Where the problem is located:
File: `/workspace/PyPSA__PyPSA__0.25/pypsa/io.py`
Function: `import_from_netcdf` (lines 642-659)
Specific problematic line: Line 656: `basename = Path(path).name`

5.3 How the test reproduces the issue:
The test creates a Network, exports it to netcdf (which returns an xarray Dataset), then tries to import that Dataset into another Network. This triggers the TypeError when `import_from_netcdf` tries to create `Path(path)` where path is a Dataset.

5.4 Best practices to consider:
- Maintain backward compatibility with existing file path usage
- Handle both string/Path inputs and xarray Dataset inputs properly
- The ImporterNetCDF class already correctly handles both cases, so we just need to fix the basename extraction
- Don't duplicate logic that already exists in ImporterNetCDF

5.5 How to fix the problem:
The fix is to conditionally extract the basename only when the path is a string or Path-like object. When it's an xarray Dataset, we can either:
- Use a default basename like "dataset" 
- Extract some meaningful name from the Dataset if possible
- Pass None as basename

Looking at the `_import_from_importer` function call, the basename is used for logging purposes. Since xarray Datasets don't have filenames, using a generic name like "dataset" or the Dataset's name attribute (if it exists) would be appropriate.

Looking at the ImporterNetCDF.__init__ method, it correctly handles both cases:
- For string/Path: opens the dataset and stores both path and ds
- For Dataset: stores the dataset directly as ds

The issue is just that we're forcing Path conversion on line 656 regardless of the input type.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Comprehensive test for the import_from_netcdf fix.

import pypsa
import tempfile
import os


def test_xarray_dataset_import():
    """Test importing from xarray Dataset instance."""
    print("Test 1: Import from xarray Dataset")
    
    # Create and populate network
    n1 = pypsa.Network()
    n1.name = "test_network"
    n1.add("Bus", "bus1", v_nom=230.0)
    n1.add("Bus", "bus2", v_nom=230.0) 
    n1.add("Line", "line1", bus0="bus1", bus1="bus2", x=0.1, r=0.01)
    
    # Export to xarray Dataset
    dataset = n1.export_to_netcdf()
    
    # Import from Dataset
    n2 = pypsa.Network()
    n2.import_from_netcdf(dataset)
    
    # Verify components were imported
    assert len(n2.buses) == 2, f"Expected 2 buses, got {len(n2.buses)}"
    assert len(n2.lines) == 1, f"Expected 1 line, got {len(n2.lines)}"
    assert "bus1" in n2.buses.index
    assert "bus2" in n2.buses.index
    assert "line1" in n2.lines.index
    
    print("✓ PASS: Import from xarray Dataset works correctly")
    return True


def test_file_path_import():
    """Test that file path imports still work (backward compatibility)."""
    print("Test 2: Import from file path")
    
    # Create network
    n1 = pypsa.Network()
    n1.name = "file_test_network"
    n1.add("Bus", "bus1", v_nom=110.0)
    
    # Test with temporary file
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.nc', delete=False) as tmp:
        tmp_path = tmp.name
        
    try:
        n1.export_to_netcdf(tmp_path)
        
        # Import from file path
        n2 = pypsa.Network()
        n2.import_from_netcdf(tmp_path)
        
        # Verify
        assert len(n2.buses) == 1, f"Expected 1 bus, got {len(n2.buses)}"
        assert "bus1" in n2.buses.index
        assert n2.name == "file_test_network"
        
        print("✓ PASS: Import from file path works correctly")
        return True
    finally:
        if os.path.exists(tmp_path):
            os.unlink(tmp_path)


def test_url_import_still_works():
    """Verify that URL imports still work (they use string paths)."""
    print("Test 3: URL/string path handling")
    
    # This test just verifies the logic doesn't break URL handling
    # We won't actually test with a real URL to avoid network dependencies
    
    fake_path = "http://example.com/network.nc"
    # This should not raise an exception in our basename logic
    # (though it would fail later when trying to access the URL)
    
    try:
        # Just test that our basename logic handles strings properly
        if isinstance(fake_path, (str, os.PathLike)):
            basename = os.path.basename(fake_path) if hasattr(os, 'PathLike') and isinstance(fake_path, os.PathLike) else fake_path.split('/')[-1]

        print("✓ PASS: String path handling works correctly")
        return True
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ FAIL: String path handling failed: {e}")
        return False


def test_complex_network_xarray():
    """Test with a more complex network exported to and from xarray."""
    print("Test 4: Complex network via xarray")
    
    # Create a more complex network
    n1 = pypsa.Network()
    n1.name = "complex_test"
    
    # Add various components
    n1.add("Carrier", "gas", color="orange")
    n1.add("Bus", "bus1", v_nom=230.0, carrier="AC")
    n1.add("Bus", "bus2", v_nom=230.0, carrier="AC") 
    n1.add("Bus", "bus3", v_nom=230.0, carrier="AC")
    n1.add("Generator", "gen1", bus="bus1", p_nom=100, marginal_cost=20)
    n1.add("Load", "load1", bus="bus2", p_set=50)
    n1.add("Line", "line1", bus0="bus1", bus1="bus2", x=0.1, r=0.01)
    n1.add("Line", "line2", bus0="bus2", bus1="bus3", x=0.15, r=0.02)
    
    # Set some snapshots for time series data
    n1.set_snapshots(range(3))
    n1.generators_t.p_set.loc[:, "gen1"] = [80, 90, 85]
    
    # Export to xarray
    dataset = n1.export_to_netcdf()
    
    # Import back
    n2 = pypsa.Network()
    n2.import_from_netcdf(dataset)
    
    # Verify all components

    assert len(n2.generators) == 1, f"Expected 1 generator, got {len(n2.generators)}"
    assert len(n2.loads) == 1, f"Expected 1 load, got {len(n2.loads)}"
    assert len(n2.lines) == 2, f"Expected 2 lines, got {len(n2.lines)}"
    assert len(n2.carriers) == 1, f"Expected 1 carrier, got {len(n2.carriers)}"

    return True


def run_all_tests():
    """Run all tests."""
    print("=" * 60)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE NETCDF IMPORT TESTS")
    print("=" * 60)
    
    tests = [
        test_xarray_dataset_import,
        test_file_path_import,
        test_url_import_still_works,

    ]

    for test in tests:
        try:
            result = test()
            results.append(result)
        except Exception as e:

            results.append(False)
        print()
    
    print("=" * 60)
    print("TEST SUMMARY:")
    passed = sum(results)
    total = len(results)
    print(f"Passed: {passed}/{total}")
    
    if passed == total:
        print("🎉 ALL TESTS PASSED!")
        return True
    else:
        print("❌ SOME TESTS FAILED!")
        return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = run_all_tests()
    exit(0 if success else 1)

function.description:
Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.

command.description: The bash command to execute. Can be empty string to view additional logs when previous exit code is `-1`. Can be `C-c` (Ctrl+C) to interrupt the currently running process. Note: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, you can use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.

is_input.description: If True, the command is an input to the running process. If False, the command is a bash command to be executed in the terminal. Default is False.

timeout.description: Optional. Sets a hard timeout in seconds for the command execution. If not provided, the command will use the default soft timeout behavior.

function.description:
This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value

function.description:
Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.

function.description:
This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value
3. Simple activities completable in minimal steps
4. Pure information exchange or discussion

Note: For single straightforward tasks, proceed with direct implementation
rather than creating tracking overhead.

## Usage Scenarios

**Scenario A: Feature Development with Validation**
User request: "Build a user authentication system with login/logout functionality.
Don't forget to include input validation and error handling!"

Response approach: I'll implement a user authentication system with comprehensive
validation. Let me organize this work systematically.

*Task breakdown includes:*
1. Design authentication API endpoints and data models
2. Implement user login/logout controllers with session management
3. Add client-side form validation and error display
4. Create backend input sanitization and security checks
5. Implement comprehensive error handling for edge cases
6. Perform integration testing and fix any issues

**Scenario B: Codebase Refactoring**
User request: "I need to update all instances of the method 'fetchData' to
'retrieveInformation' throughout the entire project"

Response approach: Let me first analyze your codebase to identify all locations
where 'fetchData' appears.

*After code analysis*

I've located 12 occurrences of 'fetchData' across 6 files in your project.
I'll create a systematic plan to update these references.

*Organized task list includes specific file-by-file updates*

**Scenario C: Multi-feature Development**
User request: "Set up a blog platform with these components: admin dashboard,
article management, comment system, and user profiles."

Response approach: I'll help build your blog platform. Let me break down these
components into manageable implementation phases.

*Creates structured plan with each feature decomposed into specific development tasks*

## Counter-examples - Direct Implementation Preferred

**Counter-example A: Simple inquiry**
User request: "What's the syntax for a for loop in JavaScript?"

Response approach: Here's how to write a for loop in JavaScript:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    console.log(array[i]);
}
```

*No task tracking needed - single informational response*

**Counter-example B: Minor modification**
User request: "Please add a docstring to the processPayment function explaining
its parameters."

Response approach: I'll add a docstring to explain the processPayment function.

*Direct edit without task tracking for simple modification*

## Status Management and Workflow

1. **Status Values**: Track work using these states:
   - todo: Not yet initiated
   - in_progress: Currently active (maintain single focus)
   - done: Successfully completed

2. **Workflow Practices**:
   - Update status dynamically as work progresses
   - Mark completion immediately upon task finish
   - Limit active work to ONE task at any given time
   - Complete current activities before initiating new ones
   - Remove obsolete tasks from tracking entirely

3. **Completion Criteria**:
   - Mark tasks as done only when fully achieved
   - Keep status as in_progress if errors, blocks, or partial completion exist
   - Create new tasks for discovered issues or dependencies
   - Never mark done when:
       - Test suites are failing
       - Implementation remains incomplete
       - Unresolved errors persist
       - Required resources are unavailable

4. **Task Organization**:
   - Write precise, actionable descriptions
   - Decompose complex work into manageable units
   - Use descriptive, clear naming conventions

When uncertain, favor using this tool. Proactive task management demonstrates
systematic approach and ensures comprehensive requirement fulfillment.

* The following binary file extensions can be viewed in Markdown format: [".xlsx", ".pptx", ".wav", ".mp3", ".m4a", ".flac", ".pdf", ".docx"]. IT DOES NOT HANDLE IMAGES.

* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

function.description:
Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.

function.description:
This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value
3. Simple activities completable in minimal steps
4. Pure information exchange or discussion

Note: For single straightforward tasks, proceed with direct implementation
rather than creating tracking overhead.

## Usage Scenarios

**Scenario A: Feature Development with Validation**
User request: "Build a user authentication system with login/logout functionality.
Don't forget to include input validation and error handling!"

Response approach: I'll implement a user authentication system with comprehensive
validation. Let me organize this work systematically.

*Task breakdown includes:*
1. Design authentication API endpoints and data models
2. Implement user login/logout controllers with session management
3. Add client-side form validation and error display
4. Create backend input sanitization and security checks
5. Implement comprehensive error handling for edge cases
6. Perform integration testing and fix any issues

**Scenario B: Codebase Refactoring**
User request: "I need to update all instances of the method 'fetchData' to
'retrieveInformation' throughout the entire project"

Response approach: Let me first analyze your codebase to identify all locations
where 'fetchData' appears.

*After code analysis*

I've located 12 occurrences of 'fetchData' across 6 files in your project.
I'll create a systematic plan to update these references.

*Organized task list includes specific file-by-file updates*

**Scenario C: Multi-feature Development**
User request: "Set up a blog platform with these components: admin dashboard,
article management, comment system, and user profiles."

Response approach: I'll help build your blog platform. Let me break down these
components into manageable implementation phases.

*Creates structured plan with each feature decomposed into specific development tasks*

## Counter-examples - Direct Implementation Preferred

**Counter-example A: Simple inquiry**
User request: "What's the syntax for a for loop in JavaScript?"

Response approach: Here's how to write a for loop in JavaScript:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    console.log(array[i]);
}
```

*No task tracking needed - single informational response*

**Counter-example B: Minor modification**
User request: "Please add a docstring to the processPayment function explaining
its parameters."

Response approach: I'll add a docstring to explain the processPayment function.

*Direct edit without task tracking for simple modification*

## Status Management and Workflow

1. **Status Values**: Track work using these states:
   - todo: Not yet initiated
   - in_progress: Currently active (maintain single focus)
   - done: Successfully completed

2. **Workflow Practices**:
   - Update status dynamically as work progresses
   - Mark completion immediately upon task finish
   - Limit active work to ONE task at any given time
   - Complete current activities before initiating new ones
   - Remove obsolete tasks from tracking entirely

3. **Completion Criteria**:
   - Mark tasks as done only when fully achieved
   - Keep status as in_progress if errors, blocks, or partial completion exist
   - Create new tasks for discovered issues or dependencies
   - Never mark done when:
       - Test suites are failing
       - Implementation remains incomplete
       - Unresolved errors persist
       - Required resources are unavailable

4. **Task Organization**:
   - Write precise, actionable descriptions
   - Decompose complex work into manageable units
   - Use descriptive, clear naming conventions

When uncertain, favor using this tool. Proactive task management demonstrates
systematic approach and ensures comprehensive requirement fulfillment.

* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The following binary file extensions can be viewed in Markdown format: [".xlsx", ".pptx", ".wav", ".mp3", ".m4a", ".flac", ".pdf", ".docx"]. IT DOES NOT HANDLE IMAGES.
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.

function.description:
Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.

function.description:
This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value
3. Simple activities completable in minimal steps
4. Pure information exchange or discussion

Note: For single straightforward tasks, proceed with direct implementation
rather than creating tracking overhead.

## Usage Scenarios

**Scenario A: Feature Development with Validation**
User request: "Build a user authentication system with login/logout functionality.
Don't forget to include input validation and error handling!"

Response approach: I'll implement a user authentication system with comprehensive
validation. Let me organize this work systematically.

*Task breakdown includes:*
1. Design authentication API endpoints and data models
2. Implement user login/logout controllers with session management
3. Add client-side form validation and error display
4. Create backend input sanitization and security checks
5. Implement comprehensive error handling for edge cases
6. Perform integration testing and fix any issues

**Scenario B: Codebase Refactoring**
User request: "I need to update all instances of the method 'fetchData' to
'retrieveInformation' throughout the entire project"

Response approach: Let me first analyze your codebase to identify all locations
where 'fetchData' appears.

*After code analysis*

I've located 12 occurrences of 'fetchData' across 6 files in your project.
I'll create a systematic plan to update these references.

*Organized task list includes specific file-by-file updates*

**Scenario C: Multi-feature Development**
User request: "Set up a blog platform with these components: admin dashboard,
article management, comment system, and user profiles."

Response approach: I'll help build your blog platform. Let me break down these
components into manageable implementation phases.

*Creates structured plan with each feature decomposed into specific development tasks*

## Counter-examples - Direct Implementation Preferred

**Counter-example A: Simple inquiry**
User request: "What's the syntax for a for loop in JavaScript?"

Response approach: Here's how to write a for loop in JavaScript:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    console.log(array[i]);
}
```

*No task tracking needed - single informational response*

**Counter-example B: Minor modification**
User request: "Please add a docstring to the processPayment function explaining
its parameters."

Response approach: I'll add a docstring to explain the processPayment function.

*Direct edit without task tracking for simple modification*

## Status Management and Workflow

1. **Status Values**: Track work using these states:
   - todo: Not yet initiated
   - in_progress: Currently active (maintain single focus)
   - done: Successfully completed

2. **Workflow Practices**:
   - Update status dynamically as work progresses
   - Mark completion immediately upon task finish
   - Limit active work to ONE task at any given time
   - Complete current activities before initiating new ones
   - Remove obsolete tasks from tracking entirely

3. **Completion Criteria**:
   - Mark tasks as done only when fully achieved
   - Keep status as in_progress if errors, blocks, or partial completion exist
   - Create new tasks for discovered issues or dependencies
   - Never mark done when:
       - Test suites are failing
       - Implementation remains incomplete
       - Unresolved errors persist
       - Required resources are unavailable

4. **Task Organization**:
   - Write precise, actionable descriptions
   - Decompose complex work into manageable units
   - Use descriptive, clear naming conventions

When uncertain, favor using this tool. Proactive task management demonstrates
systematic approach and ensures comprehensive requirement fulfillment.

Custom editing tool for viewing, creating and editing files in plain-text format
* State is persistent across command calls and discussions with the user
* If `path` is a text file, `view` displays the result of applying `cat -n`. If `path` is a directory, `view` lists non-hidden files and directories up to 2 levels deep
* The following binary file extensions can be viewed in Markdown format: [".xlsx", ".pptx", ".wav", ".mp3", ".m4a", ".flac", ".pdf", ".docx"]. IT DOES NOT HANDLE IMAGES.
* The `create` command cannot be used if the specified `path` already exists as a file
* If a `command` generates a long output, it will be truncated and marked with `<response clipped>`
* The `undo_edit` command will revert the last edit made to the file at `path`
* This tool can be used for creating and editing files in plain-text format.


Before using this tool:
1. Use the view tool to understand the file's contents and context
2. Verify the directory path is correct (only applicable when creating new files):
   - Use the view tool to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

When making edits:
   - Ensure the edit results in idiomatic, correct code
   - Do not leave the code in a broken state
   - Always use absolute file paths (starting with /)

CRITICAL REQUIREMENTS FOR USING THIS TOOL:

1. EXACT MATCHING: The `old_str` parameter must match EXACTLY one or more consecutive lines from the file, including all whitespace and indentation. The tool will fail if `old_str` matches multiple locations or doesn't match exactly with the file content.

2. UNIQUENESS: The `old_str` must uniquely identify a single instance in the file:
   - Include sufficient context before and after the change point (3-5 lines recommended)
   - If not unique, the replacement will not be performed

3. REPLACEMENT: The `new_str` parameter should contain the edited lines that replace the `old_str`. Both strings must be different.

Remember: when making multiple file edits in a row to the same file, you should prefer to send all edits in a single message with multiple calls to this tool, rather than multiple messages with a single call each.

Looking at the code, I can see two clear issues:

1. **Line 357 Bug**: In the mother's validation block, it's checking `donor.father_pk` instead of `donor.mother_pk`. This is clearly a copy-paste error.

2. **The actual issue described**: The bug report mentions that "InconsistentPedigreeException maybe raised incorrectly" when a father is missing. Looking at the logic, the issue seems to be that when a father or mother is missing from the pedigree (but referenced), it raises an exception. However, in real-world scenarios, families can be incomplete - parents might not be available or sequenced.

Looking at the error message and logic:
- Line 350: `if not pedigree.pk_to_donor.get(donor.father_pk, None):` - This checks if the father is in the same pedigree
- Line 357: `if not pedigree.pk_to_donor.get(donor.father_pk, None):` - BUG: Should be checking `donor.mother_pk`

But the deeper issue mentioned in the bug report is that this validation might be too strict. Let me think about when this could happen legitimately:

1. A child has a fatherPk set but the father is not in the same pedigree (maybe not sequenced)
2. This could be valid in incomplete families

However, looking at the test case, the exception is EXPECTED to be raised when family definitions are inconsistent. So the validation logic might be correct, but there's definitely the bug in line 357.

def test_reported_issue():

Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.

function.description:
This tool provides structured task management capabilities for development workflows.
It enables systematic tracking of work items, progress monitoring, and efficient
organization of complex development activities.

The tool maintains visibility into project status and helps communicate
progress effectively to users.

## Application Guidelines

Utilize this tool in the following situations:

1. Multi-phase development work - When projects involve multiple sequential or
   parallel activities
2. Complex implementation tasks - Work requiring systematic planning and
   coordination across multiple components
3. Explicit user request for task organization - When users specifically ask
   for structured task management
4. Multiple concurrent requirements - When users present several work items
   that need coordination
5. Project initiation - Capture and organize user requirements at project start
6. Work commencement - Update task status to in_progress before beginning
   implementation. Maintain focus by limiting active work to one task
7. Task completion - Update status to done and identify any additional work
   that emerged during implementation

## Situations Where Tool Usage Is Unnecessary

Avoid using this tool when:

1. Single atomic tasks that require no decomposition
2. Trivial operations where tracking adds no organizational value
3. Simple activities completable in minimal steps
4. Pure information exchange or discussion

Note: For single straightforward tasks, proceed with direct implementation
rather than creating tracking overhead.

## Usage Scenarios

**Scenario A: Feature Development with Validation**
User request: "Build a user authentication system with login/logout functionality.
Don't forget to include input validation and error handling!"

Response approach: I'll implement a user authentication system with comprehensive
validation. Let me organize this work systematically.

*Task breakdown includes:*
1. Design authentication API endpoints and data models
2. Implement user login/logout controllers with session management
3. Add client-side form validation and error display
4. Create backend input sanitization and security checks
5. Implement comprehensive error handling for edge cases
6. Perform integration testing and fix any issues

**Scenario B: Codebase Refactoring**
User request: "I need to update all instances of the method 'fetchData' to
'retrieveInformation' throughout the entire project"

Response approach: Let me first analyze your codebase to identify all locations
where 'fetchData' appears.

*After code analysis*

I've located 12 occurrences of 'fetchData' across 6 files in your project.
I'll create a systematic plan to update these references.

*Organized task list includes specific file-by-file updates*

**Scenario C: Multi-feature Development**
User request: "Set up a blog platform with these components: admin dashboard,
article management, comment system, and user profiles."

Response approach: I'll help build your blog platform. Let me break down these
components into manageable implementation phases.

*Creates structured plan with each feature decomposed into specific development tasks*

## Counter-examples - Direct Implementation Preferred

**Counter-example A: Simple inquiry**
User request: "What's the syntax for a for loop in JavaScript?"

Response approach: Here's how to write a for loop in JavaScript:

```javascript
for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    console.log(array[i]);
}
```

*No task tracking needed - single informational response*

**Counter-example B: Minor modification**
User request: "Please add a docstring to the processPayment function explaining
its parameters."

Response approach: I'll add a docstring to explain the processPayment function.

*Direct edit without task tracking for simple modification*

## Status Management and Workflow

1. **Status Values**: Track work using these states:
   - todo: Not yet initiated
   - in_progress: Currently active (maintain single focus)
   - done: Successfully completed

2. **Workflow Practices**:
   - Update status dynamically as work progresses
   - Mark completion immediately upon task finish
   - Limit active work to ONE task at any given time
   - Complete current activities before initiating new ones
   - Remove obsolete tasks from tracking entirely

3. **Completion Criteria**:
   - Mark tasks as done only when fully achieved
   - Keep status as in_progress if errors, blocks, or partial completion exist
   - Create new tasks for discovered issues or dependencies
   - Never mark done when:
       - Test suites are failing
       - Implementation remains incomplete
       - Unresolved errors persist
       - Required resources are unavailable

4. **Task Organization**:
   - Write precise, actionable descriptions
   - Decompose complex work into manageable units
   - Use descriptive, clear naming conventions

When uncertain, favor using this tool. Proactive task management demonstrates
systematic approach and ensures comprehensive requirement fulfillment.

### 1.1-1.3 Problem Analysis

The issue describes a problem with the credentials file parsing in the ConductR CLI. 

**Problem Summary:** 
The credentials file parser can only handle one section, but users need to define multiple credential sections for different hosts/realms. When multiple sections are present, the parsing fails and prevents fetching ConductR artifacts from Bintray.

**Technical Details:**
- **File name:** `.lightbend/commercial.credentials`
- **Command that fails:** `sandbox run 2.1.1 --feature visualization`
- **Error message:** "Unable to fetch ConductR core artifact 2.1.1 from Bintray"
- **Expected format:** Multiple sections with realm/host/user/password combinations
- **Current behavior:** Only first section is processed correctly

### 1.4 Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a credentials file with multiple sections (as shown in the issue)
2. Run `sandbox run 2.1.1 --feature visualization`
3. Observe the error about unable to fetch ConductR core artifact
4. Remove the second section and retry - it should work

### 1.5 Best Practices
- Support standard INI file format with multiple sections
- Handle backward compatibility with single-section files
- Proper error handling for malformed credentials
- Clear logging when credentials are loaded/used

   287	
   288	CLI releases to the pip3 repository can be performed completely from the GitHub project page. Follow these steps to cut a release:
   289	
   290	1. Edit `conductr_cli/__init__.py <conductr_cli/__init__.py>`_ file to contain the version to be released.
   291	2. Create a new release on the `Github releases page <https://github.com/typesafehub/conductr-cli/releases>`_.
   292	
   293	After CI build is finished for the tagged commit, new version will automatically be deployed to PyPi repository.
   294	
   295	**Native**
   296	
   297	Ensure correct system requirement is used for each target platform.
   298	
   299	For MacOS:
   300	
   301	* OSX version ``10.11``: native executables built on ``10.11`` will be compatible with ``10.12``, but the reverse is not true.
   302	* Python version ``3.5``.
   303	
   304	For Linux:
   305	
   306	* Ubuntu version ``14.04.5 LTS``.
   307	* Python version ``3.4``.
   308	
   309	For Windows:
   310	
   311	* Windows 7
   312	* Python version ``3.5``.
   313	* 7Zip executable from http://www.7-zip.org/download.html required to build zip file on the command line. When installing 7Zip, ensure the 7z.exe is available on the Windows ``%PATH%``.
   314	
   315	Pyinstaller version ``3.2.1`` or above is required. Please visit http://www.pyinstaller.org/ to obtain instructions on how to install it.
   316	
   317	Ensure the native executables are built from tagged release commit.
   318	
   319	Continue to build native packages.
   320	
   321	For MacOS and Linux:
   322	
   323	.. code:: bash
   324	
   325	    sh package-native-zip.sh [release-version-number]
   326	
   327	
   328	For Windows perform the following steps.
   329	
   330	Open a DOS prompt, and then execute the following command.
   331	
   332	.. code:: bash
   333	
   334	    set CONDUCTR_HOST=192.168.10.1
   335	
   336	For those using Windows VM, the local sandbox address ``192.168.10.1`` can be used - ensure the sandbox on the host machine has been started before proceeding further. This will allow the CLI on the Windows VM to connect to the ConductR running on the host machine.
   337	
   338	If you wish to use ConductR running from a different host, replace ``192.168.10.1`` accordingly.
   339	
   340	.. code:: bash
   341	
   342	    package-native-zip.bat [release-version-number]
   343	
   344	
   345	The ``package-native-zip.sh`` and ``package-native-zip.bat`` follow performs the following steps.
   346	
   347	First it builds the native executables.
   348	
   349	.. code:: bash
   350	
   351	    pyinstaller --onefile conductr_cli/conduct.py
   352	    pyinstaller --hidden-import psutil --onefile conductr_cli/sandbox.py    
   353	    pyinstaller --onefile conductr_cli/shazar.py
   354	    pyinstaller --onefile conductr_cli/bndl.py
   355	    
   356	This will result in standalone images for your current environment being created in a ``dist`` folder.
   357	
   358	It will ensure correct versions are built. This is done by comparing the version number from the output of the commands below with the input to the script. If there's a mismatch, the script will exit with failure.
   359	
   360	.. code:: bash
   361	
   362	    ./dist/sandbox version
   363	    ./dist/conduct version
   364	
   365	For MacOS and Linux, perform sanity check by running:
   366	
   367	.. code:: bash
   368	
   369	    ./dist/sandbox run 2.0.0 -f visualization
   370	    ./dist/conduct info
   371	    ./dist/shazar -h
   372	    ./dist/bndl -h    
   373	
   374	For Windows, perform the following since the ``sandbox`` command is not supported:
   375	
   376	.. code:: bash
   377	
   378	    ./dist/conduct info
   379	    ./dist/shazar -h
   380	    ./dist/bndl -h

## Phase 5. FIX ANALYSIS

### 5.1 Problem Statement
The `load_bintray_credentials` function in `bintray_resolver.py` cannot handle credentials files with multiple sections. When multiple sections exist with the same keys (`realm`, `host`, `user`, `password`), later sections overwrite earlier ones, causing incorrect credentials to be used.

### 5.2 Problem Location  
The issue is in `/workspace/typesafehub__conductr-cli__1.2/conductr_cli/resolvers/bintray_resolver.py`, specifically in the `load_bintray_credentials` function (lines 160-188).

### 5.3 How the Test Reproduces the Issue
The reproduction script shows that when a credentials file contains multiple sections, the function returns the credentials from the last section rather than the appropriate section for the target host.

### 5.4 Best Practices for the Fix
1. **Backward compatibility**: Must continue to work with existing single-section credential files
2. **Proper INI file parsing**: Should parse sections correctly using standard INI format
3. **Host-based selection**: Should return credentials appropriate for the target host
4. **Minimal changes**: Should not break existing functionality
5. **Clear error handling**: Should maintain proper error reporting

### 5.5 How to Fix the Problem
The solution is to:
1. Modify `load_bintray_credentials` to parse the credentials file as proper INI sections
2. When multiple sections exist, select the appropriate one based on the target host
3. For backward compatibility, treat the entire file as one section if no section headers are present
4. Return the correct credentials for `dl.bintray.com` (downloads) vs `api.bintray.com` (API calls)

The challenge is that the function currently returns a single `(realm, user, password)` tuple, but we need to make it smart enough to return the right credentials for the right host.

Execute a bash command in the terminal within a persistent shell session.


### Command Execution
* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.
* Persistent session: Commands execute in a persistent shell session where environment variables, virtual environments, and working directory persist between commands.
* Soft timeout: Commands have a soft timeout of 10 seconds, once that's reached, you have the option to continue or interrupt the command (see section below for details)

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.
* For commands that may run for a long time (e.g. installation or testing commands), or commands that run for a fixed amount of time (e.g. sleep), you should set the "timeout" parameter of your function call to an appropriate value.
* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:
  - Send empty `command` to retrieve additional logs
  - Send text (set `command` to the text) to STDIN of the running process
  - Send control commands like `C-c` (Ctrl+C), `C-d` (Ctrl+D), or `C-z` (Ctrl+Z) to interrupt the process
  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.
